newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin says no turning back on promises.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin says no turning back on promises.

text.p: French Socialist Lionel Jospin, in his first policy address since becoming prime minister, has promised there will be no turning back on his ambitious agenda and no renunciation of his campaign promises.

But Jospin has given himself breathing room by moving quickly on vows that cost little or nothing and putting off the costlier pledges that he cannot afford or which could derail Paris' drive towards a single European currency.

His programme will be carried out gradually, over a five-year period, "without pause, without retreat, without repudiation," Jospin said in his first major policy address since taking office 2-1/2 weeks ago.
But it will require "time and perseverance," he added.

The message, later endorsed by the National Assembly in a vote of confidence, was clearly meant to contrast with the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, who reversed course after two years, and conservative President Jacques Chirac, who did so after just six months in office.

France's restive labour unions, which could boost Jospin's chances for success by holding off on labour disruption which dogged his centre-right predecessors, gave a cautious green light to the prime minister's charted course, but also expressed reservations.

They praised his pledge to make a clean break with the previous government in, for example, urging immigration and justice reforms, calling off further cuts in civil service posts and boosting back-to-school and housing allowances.

Jospin pledged to ease hard-line immigration and nationality laws enacted earlier this year and to free the justice system from political meddling by isolating investigating judges from outside interference.
But the unions criticised a lack of detail on future salary talks and his decision to raise the minimum wage by four percent when the unions and Communists had called for an eight percent increase.

"We found in this speech a certain willingness to take into account what the voters have expressed...but strong intervention by salaried workers remains more than ever necessary to achieve our aspirations," The Communist-dominated CGT union said in a veiled warning statement.

Some financial analysts praised Jospin's vagueness on specifics on how and when he planned to fulfil potentially costly pledges to create 700,000 jobs and reduce the working week by four hours without a loss of pay.

They also welcomed his decision to delay revisions in the 1997 state budget and put off a promised national conference on wages, jobs and working hours until after a planned audit of public finances, due to be completed in mid-July.
These analysts said the moves showed that Jospin, who said he feared the state of public finances was "serious", wished to take a slow and cautious approach to sensitive spending decisions.
But others said the delays would leave him little time to rectify French finances if major problems turned up.

The audit is expected to show how far France has strayed from reducing its deficit to the goal of three percent of gross domestic product to qualify for European economic and monetary union from 1999.
Jospin said he was committed to shifting to the euro single currency on time but significantly he made no mention of meeting the criteria.
